source_refs.note: Topic printed 1.1.1.1 What is a Class Diagram? with Fig. 1.10 (PDF 22-23, printed 19-20).

blocks.text: A class diagram is like a map that shows how things are organized in a system, just like how you organize your room. It helps us see what's in each box (like your toys, books, or clothes) and how these boxes are related.
In the example of s organizing your room:

items: Room: Represents the overall space encompassing all other elements, analogous to the main structure in a class diagram.
Box: Serves as a container within the room, akin to a class in a diagram.
Attributes: Each box contains specific items, such as a 'ToyBox' holding toys or a 'BookBox' containing books.
Methods: Boxes can perform actions like 'open' or 'close,' similar to methods in a class diagram that define what the box can do.
Specific Boxes: Examples of specialized boxes include a 'ToyBox' for toys, a 'BookBox' for books, and a 'ClothesBox' for clothes, representing distinct instances of the general 'Box' class.

blocks.text: So, a class diagram is simply a way to organize and show how different parts of a system (like your room) work together, making it easier to understand everything at a glance as show in Figure 1.10.

blocks.alt: Class boxes: Room (-name: String, -size: String) at the top, joined by a plain line to Box (-label: String, -contents: String). Below, ToyBox (-toys: List), BookBox (-books: List) and ClothesBox (-clothes: List) each have a line ending in a hollow triangle that points up to Box.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.10: Class Diagram for Organizing Your Room (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.10, with UML inheritance arrowheads).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 1.10 uses open arrowheads from ToyBox, BookBox and ClothesBox to Box; in UML inheritance is shown with a hollow triangle arrowhead, as drawn above.
